I'm curious if there is a comprehensive and concise document of the type theory that is modeled versus the one Lean implements, with all gaps explained very clearly. I did something like this with my students in the course I taught last semester for the proof assistant we built, for example: https://github.com/nicegeo/nicegeo/blob/main/METATHEORY.md

Even though for us, a verified kernel was wildly out of scope, I made sure we had this because the most consequential bugs often manifest in these gaps

The approach lean4lean takes is a bit simpler than my masters thesis: There is one typing relation, the "idealized" one, which satisfies transitivity and subject reduction and is not decidable. Then there is a kernel program, which is sound but not complete (or at least it should be, and most soundness bugs are in this part). So recast in these terms, the question is: where is the lean checker not complete?

There are a few known places:

  • The checking of unit-like types is not complete. It checks only Unit (and similar inductives) and propositions, but it should also include pi types whose codomain is unit-like and structures containing only unit-like types.
  • The level algorithm is incomplete. Lean4lean has a potential replacement algorithm that should be complete.
  • Lean does not compute through some large eliminating subsingleton inductives, including Acc and Quot. For Acc in particular this would cause lean to not terminate when typechecking some things, so it is understandable that lean doesn't do this, but it could at least be gated in a more principled way, e.g. by having a fuel amount controlling unfolding.

This is all I can recall; it's plausible that if you fix those then you can prove a completeness theorem for typechecking.
How are nested inductives handled?
badly :)

it still remains to determine how to even specify what a nested inductive is supposed to be, and until that work is done we can't prove either soundness or completeness. @Arthur Adjedj has expressed some interest in working on the nested inductive spec

I would argue that extending a "naive" strict positivity criteria for non-nested types to handle nesteds will not be absurdly hard. In particular, a formal specification of Rocq’s nested positivity criteria already exists, and Lean’s resembles it closely (I can take the time to explicit the differences if someone is interested in looking into this). I plan on working on either a specification for base inductive types or for nesteds based on existing Rocq work in a month or so, depending of the state of things by that time.
Is there a model where strict positivity is intrinsic? Something like https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.08837

Kovacs’ work on theories of signatures is, to my knowledge, the most "intrinsic" presentation of inductive types around. Lean4Lean relies on extrinsic properties anyway, so the inductive formalisms will surely do so too

Cool. Curious how to classify those kinds of gaps and document them. Happy to help with some documentation and related work for that (I have strep though so may take some time) if you know where those kinds of features fall

if you talk to @Meven Lennon-Bertrand he'll argue for having a proof also of "negative soundness", i.e. if the typechecker says a typing or defeq doesn't hold then it doesn't, even if there is an in between possibility for nontermination. Currently I make no attempt to prove negative provability facts, but that's basically how you would establish completeness
Meven's paper What Does It Take to Certify a Conversion Checker? talks about what you need to do to certify negative soundness properties

A quick command I did seems to indicate nested types are used in a fair amount of places:

import Lean
import Mathlib

open Lean Elab Meta Command

run_cmd liftTermElabM do
  let env ← getEnv
  let mut nestedTypes : List Name := []
  for (declName,_) in env.constants do
    try
      let indVal ← getConstInfoInduct declName
      if indVal.numNested != 0 then
        nestedTypes := declName::nestedTypes
    catch _ => continue
  logInfo m!"number of nested types {nestedTypes.length} : \n {nestedTypes}"

The main point of nested inductive types is that they allow for modularly reusing existing APIs. In theory, you could replace any nested inductive type to a mutual inductive type, similarly to what the kernel does internally, but that would imply having to duplicate any API around the type you nested under for the use-case of this new one, leading to a lot of duplicated code and complications. Lean 3 used to not have nested types at the type theory level, and the need for those seems to have manifested clearly enough for them to become part of the kernel when transitioning to Lean 4. I don't think getting rid of them would be a step in the right direction.
I can think of two related uses : unbounded fan-in circuits (see my library), and, well, trees.

I was considering proposing that checkers could track which feature are used by a development, and maybe AI based math projects would just have a policy of not using nested inductives. Many of the ones listed by Arthur are in meta code and would not show up in the exported slice of a main theorem. But maybe this direction is more confusing than helpful to users.

I already avoid nested inductives in all languages whenever tractable. But they show up a lot with programming language and compiler verification and metatheory, and rose trees etc. Ideally, they should not add any expressive power over vanilla inductives, but the transformation is wildly nontrivial to do manually and as actually implemented, that statement isn't even true anyways

I think in an ideal world it might be that they are implemented as sugar that elaborate to vanilla inductives (with mutual inductives as a step in between), much like primitive pattern matching is a mistake and Lean did that right. But this would be a major change to the scope of types supported, based on extremely recent type theory results, using transformations that would be wildly nontrivial to implement
But in the world we live in I think we just need to reimplement nested inductives to be the intended fragment to begin with based on those recent results
Disclaimer: I am still very sick with strep, I may say incorrect or confusing things the next day or two

@Talia Ringer Leo's latest blog post says

This way, lean-inductive-models also addresses a concern raised on social media and in public discussions: whether the theory behind Lean's inductive types is fully understood. The same derivation demonstrates that the constructions Lean uses are well understood.

just so you know....

I would definitely not classify that Claudeslop as demonstrating any kind
of "understanding"

@Talia Ringer :
Sebastian Ullrich said:

The claimed gain in understanding is simply this: the set of inductives accepted by lean-inductive-models, which so far has matched that of leanchecker, can be constructed from first principles. There is no claim that this corresponds to some formal model of inductives or on properties other than soundness (i.e. the focus of the postmortem).
Maybe the blog post needs updating since the readme has been updated on lean-inductive-models.

Yeah absolutely needs updating, see also the rest of that thread. It is a certifying approach which is certainly useful! But it provides no gain in "understanding" even about soundness. What it can provide is, on a case-by-case basis, additional guarantees that make the user more confident in soundness. Which is useful! But it is absolutely not anything more than that, and Leo writes as if somehow this is sufficient to say we know what Lean is doing for all inductive types Lean implements! We certainly do not!

I think the "soundness" claim, while poorly worded, means this. If the user uses Comparator with all available checkers (which is quickly becoming the gold standard), then as long as lean-inductive-models is one of the checkers, then one can't exploit more complicated inductive types to prove False (at least in a way that can't be done without those types), since those complicated types are reduced to simpler types in lean-inductive-models. Maybe this approach isn't complete and some proof which passes the normal lean kernel would fail lean-inductive-models, but it seems to work in practice. And the soundness situation for the simpler types is much better understood (closely matching Mario's thesis and what has been formalized already in a branch of lean4lean-model). Or at least that is how I read the situation (but I'm reading between the lines of the blog post).

I mean, OK, but Lean4Lean can't be finished until you actually have a model of inductive types that isn't just doing translation validation, and kernel implementations will continue to copy each others' potentially-buggy implementations until there is actually a spec for Lean's type theory that reflects reality

This is a useful thing to do, but Leo really needs to be careful what he writes in public-facing blog posts. I'm working with a couple of funders right now to support this and other work, and blog posts like that make it less likely the funders agree to actually support it.

yes and no, right? You can have two lean4leans? One which covers inductive types and one which covers the fragment which comes after lean-inductive-model, no? I don't know if Mario is interested in this, but in my very limited spare time, I'm seeing if I can vibe code a complete verified pipeline along those lines as a proof of concept. (I don't know if I'll succeed.)
Sure, again, it is useful but it is not the end game
And RE "reality": if lean-inductive-model is part of the usual workflow then it becomes reality, no?
But not the end game, no.

Sure, but it does not have a model of what inductive types really are, so the language of Lean's actual implemented type theory is not specified. Which means other kernels are more likely to copy over the buggy implementations from other kernels. This may include bugs in surprising places, like with definitional equality (again, again, again). But in general it is just bad if there is any encouragement at all for Lean kernel implementations to copy any part of what they do from one another. Which is why there should be a complete, accurate model of the type theory.

It will increase my confidence for now in lack of reward hacking by AI agents exploiting not-yet-known bugs in the inductive fragment of Lean if I am able to use it in a straightforward way when checking those, and chain it with a limited version of something like Lean4Lean. But speaking as if it makes the type theory work unneeded and aids at all in any "understanding" is not correct

I understand the situation is urgent enough that faster responses that don't fully solve the problem are needed, but we should not let those stop people from funding and working on fully solving the problem

Nobody and nothing is stopping anyone from funding anything or fully solving the problem because of this tool or because of one sentence in a subsection in a blog post. Can we please all calm down a bit again?

What's I would find much more interesting than lawyering over the impact of this tool on understanding of the issue would be a discussion on whether it factors the problem in a helpful way. Can we “fully solve the problem” for the target theory of the inductive models (fixed signature of types, but a form of extensionality) more easily than for Lean's theory?
(Best discussed in #lean4lean > lean-inductive-models probably.)

Funders who see the creator of Lean say something they interpret as "this problem is solved" in a public announcement are going to view an application for serious money to attack this problem may well not bother to read fine print and think twice before pouring money onto what they think they have been told is a solved problem. The extent to which this is believed to be plausible or true will almost surely vary; no one is complaining about the repo being accurate, but about the much more public statement in a non-technical format.

You can't both complain that social media posts on Lean's soundness are hurting Lean by spreading negative misinformation (as argued in the document on how to report soundness), and also argue that writing social media posts painting other's work as useless is not hurting them. The restraint cannot possibly go only one way.

FWIW I was interviewed by a Quanta journalist about Lean soundness bugs this morning, and I was very thorough and fair, and also referred her to several of you and to papers and/or products you all have built for further discussion. Some topics covered:

  1. The de Bruijn Criterion for proof assistant design
  2. The history of kernel bugs in a human context
  3. Why they matter so much more in an AI context
  4. Lean4Lean
  5. Why to model the whole type theory
  6. What folks can still do before modeling the whole type theory
  7. Why inductive types are conceptually hard
  8. Why inductive types are practically hard to implement
  9. The pragmatics of the de Bruijn Criterion
  10. Fire triangles and other surprising ways things can break

Referred to relevant folks for further context on some of those points (including @Mario Carneiro on number 4, @Joachim Breitner on number 6, and Kiran on this specific bug) so I hope she will be thorough and reach out to you all

For what it’s worth I also had an email exchange with probably the same journalist. I didn’t give an interview (for personal reasons), but i gave references to others and a few thoughts. If someone wants to know, happy to DM my exchange.
